reason: Broken on wording, in the exact place the verifier chose to intervene. The note says a comma after All the same “was missing and is restored”, resting on two reproductions said to be independent. Both halves of that are wrong. (1) The two reproductions are not independent: Letters of Note and HeadButler carry the same distinctive typo, “it flowers only once every four years, Now, I am already a very old woman”, a comma where the sentence plainly ends. Texts that share a typo share a source. (2) They do not read the printed 1961 translation. I reached the printed pages through archive.org's inside-the-book index (openlibrary.org/search/inside), which returns matched lines from scans that are lending-restricted for reading. In breakofdaynovel00cole, the Farrar, Straus and Cudahy 1961 McLeod first American printing named in the evidence, the letter reads “...delights me, and I'm touched that you should ask me to come and see her. All the same I'm not going to accept your kind invitation, for the time being at any rate.” The second Break of Day printing, breakofday0000cole, reads the same: “and I'm touched that you should ask me to come and see her. All the same I'm not going to accept your kind invitation, for the time being at any rate.” No comma after All the same, and the earlier sentence is “ask me to come and see her”, not “ask me to come see her” as the web copies have it. The web wording with the comma and with “come see her” does exist in print, in Gigi and Selected Writings (gigiselectedwrit0000cole), which is a different setting of the text: the verifier's sources reproduce that, not the 1961 edition their source line names. So the comma is not a restoration, it is an insertion into a named translation, which is minting. The rest of the quotation survives the same test and should be kept: “probably” is confirmed in both Break of Day scans against the “finally” found in two blog quotations, matching the French probablement; “It's a very rare plant I've been given, and I'm told that in our climate it flowers only once every four years.” is confirmed in breakofday0000cole and breakofdaynovel00cole, and the full stop after four years is right, the web comma being the typo. Everything else checks out: the edition is real (Open Library OL5828941M, Farrar, Straus and Cudahy, 1961, 143 pp., Translated by Enid McLeod, Introd. by Glenway Wescott); the letter does open the novel; Sido is the writer and Colette's second husband the addressee; shipped.js returns not shipped, nothing near, Colette 0 of 3, not banned, and no second Colette in April; it is in scope and publishable and on theme. Two smaller faults to fix while the line is open. The source line puts the speaker after the translation, “(trans. Enid McLeod, 1961) (Sido, the narrator's mother)”, where the landed precedent carried in this very brief, 03-cfl-09, puts the speaker first and its note says so in as many words. And the note should stop claiming two independent reproductions and say plainly what is now known: the wording is witnessed in the printed 1961 text through a full-text index of the scan, not by opening the page, and the punctuation of the excerpt is therefore reported, not seen.

Enid McLeod, 1961), with the quotation as printed: “All the same I’m not going to accept your kind invitation, for the time being at any rate. The reason is that my pink cactus is probably going to flower. It’s a very rare plant I’ve been given, and I’m told that in our climate it flowers only once every four years.”
